Agent Protocols and Tools::Model Context.sourceTitle: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
Agent Protocols and Tools::Model Context.summary: MCP is an open standard that lets AI applications connect to external systems through a common protocol. It supports data sources, callable tools, and reusable prompt-based workflows.
Agent Protocols and Tools::Model Context.explanation: MCP uses a client–server design for exchanging context between AI applications and external systems. A host can create clients that connect to servers exposing tools, resources, and prompts; the protocol uses JSON-RPC messages and capability negotiation so each side can advertise supported features.

example.title: Calling an MCP tool
example.code: const result = await client.callTool({ name: "search", arguments: { query: "MCP" } });
example.explanation: An MCP client asks a connected server to execute a named tool with structured arguments.

useCases.title: Context retrieval
useCases.scenario: An AI assistant needs information from local files or databases.

useCases.title: Tool execution
useCases.scenario: An agent must search, calculate, call an API, or perform another operation.

useCases.title: Prompt workflows
useCases.scenario: An application offers repeatable, parameterized interaction patterns.

interview.question: What problem does MCP solve?
interview.answer: MCP standardizes integration between LLM applications and external data sources and tools. It defines shared primitives such as resources, prompts, and tools, allowing applications to reuse integrations instead of implementing a separate connector for each service.
interview.followUp: How are supported features discovered? During capability negotiation, clients and servers declare the features they support, such as tools, resource subscriptions, or prompt templates.

interview.question: Describe MCP's architecture.
interview.answer: MCP follows a host–client–server architecture. A host can run multiple client instances, and those clients connect to servers that expose capabilities through the protocol.
interview.followUp: Why separate clients from servers? The separation isolates application concerns and creates clear security boundaries between the host and external integrations.

interview.question: What protocol and primitives does MCP use?
interview.answer: MCP is built on JSON-RPC and focuses on context exchange and sampling coordination between clients and servers. Its core primitives include tools, resources, prompts, and notifications.
interview.followUp: What distinguishes the primitives? Tools are executable capabilities, resources provide contextual information, and prompts represent reusable interaction templates.

keyPoints: MCP gives AI applications a common way to connect with external systems rather than requiring bespoke integration conventions.
The protocol covers three useful integration categories: data sources, callable tools, and reusable workflows or prompts.
A single host may coordinate several MCP clients, allowing it to connect independently to multiple servers or integrations.
JSON-RPC provides the message foundation while MCP concentrates on exchanging context and coordinating sampling.
Each request carries the information needed to interpret it, which avoids relying on hidden protocol session state.
gotchas: Treat requests as self-contained: do not assume the protocol maintains implicit conversational state between messages.
Clients must account for server capabilities instead of assuming every server provides every MCP primitive.
